content.title: Louisville Kings' opener shows UFL is no gimmick — it's real football
content.text: Temperatures in the low 40s fittingly brought out the bubble jackets and hoodies, blankets and beanie caps for many in the crowd of 14,034 in Lynn Family Stadium for the Louisville Kings' debut in the United Football League.Everything about the game felt like a late October fall night in the thick of football season. And even though the Kings fell short in a 15-13 loss to Birmingham, Louisville has a winner.AdvertisementProfessional football has arrived, and the city embraced it like it has been here all along."Everything that we're doing is brand-new to us right now," said Kings head coach Chris Redman, the former Male High and University of Louisville quarterback. "It's a learning experience for all of us."1 / 14Louisville Kings begin season with game against Birmingham StallionsJohn Schweizer attends the first tailgate for a Louisville Kings football game at Lynn Family Stadium. March 27, 20262 / 14Louisville Kings begin season with game against Birmingham StallionsRob Robinson, left, and Steve Simms say their Kings flag is expected to arrive tomorrow as they attend the first tailgate for a Louisville Kings football game at Lynn Family Stadium. March 27, 202614 / 14Louisville Kings begin season with game against Birmingham StallionsThe Louisville Kings Corner podcast was at the first tailgate for a Louisville Kings football game at Lynn Family Stadium. March 27, 2026Any lover of football who has seen the UFL being broadcast, but not really watched it, will like that the Kings have to deliver.There's real talent in the UFL.Super Bowl winners, like Birmingham's Jaydon Mickens, who caught passes from Tom Brady on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Players — like Kings running back Benny Snell, who played at Kentucky — who have spent time on NFL rosters and may be looking for a second chance. There are others, like Kings quarterback Jason Bean, trying to show enough potential to make a 53-man roster down the line.AdvertisementThere's innovation, too.The national broadcast on Fox included live listens to communication between the coaches and coordinators, calling plays and speaking with referees. The drone camera flying around could sometimes seem like an electric gnat to those in the stadium, but it provides a unique perspective when used in the game.Some of the rules will take a little getting used to, like having one-, two- or three-point options after touchdowns and four-point field goal of 60 yards or more. One rule in particular fans will grow to love is that there’s no punting once the team crosses the 50-yard line, except in the final two minutes of a half.But there is nothing gimmicky about it.Louisville Kings’ Kaden Prather caught the ball for a first down against Birmingham Stallions’ Alex Cook (30) and Hudson Clark in a United Football League game at Lynn Family Stadium. March 27, 2026Football fans in the city, normally split between UofL and Kentucky in college or the Cincinnati Bengals and Indianapolis Colts in the NFL, can unite behind the Kings.AdvertisementAt least of few already showed they were unified in how they greeted the Stallions. Mickens lamented his teammates having beer thrown on them. In a backhanded way, even that was a nice touch, indicative of a well-established fan base despite the Kings being one of three new franchises in the league this season."We love the back and forth," said Mickens, who responded with a game-high nine catches for 103 yards. "We don't like beer thrown on us, but we do love the crowd."There will be much nicer nights in the spring, probably as soon as their next home game on April 10 against the Orlando Storm. So there will be plenty of chances to build off what was started on Friday.The Kings can get better, too.AdvertisementRunning back Ian Wheeler fumbled at the Birmingham 1-yard line in the closing seconds before halftime with a chance to give the Kings the lead. Instead, they trailed 9-7 at the break. Jaden Shirley's 39-yard kickoff return had the Kings set up at the 50 with less than two minutes left in the game, needing only a short drive for a game-winning field goal. Bean threw into double coverage and was intercepted to essentially seal the loss.Despite the miscues, Redman believes Louisville has something brewing."We're excited about what the potential is," Redman said. "If these people had fun today, we're going to give them a lot better shows in the future."There's no gimmick in that.AdvertisementReach sports columnist C.L.
